meta_description: A free printable chore chart for a 12 year old with an editable money column and weekly total, plus a dad of four on pricing chores and allowance fairly.
h1: Chore Chart for a 12-Year-Old (With a Money Column)
intro: Twelve is a funny in-between age. Your kid isn't a little one you're cleaning up after anymore, but they're not quite the teenager who'd rather you forgot they had chores at all. They can handle almost anything around the house now, and they're suddenly very interested in having their own spending money. That combination is exactly what this page is built for. The free printable below is a chore chart for a 12-year-old with an editable money column and a running weekly total, so you can set dollar amounts that make sense for your family right on the page. I'm Andrew, and my wife and I are the SproutChores family, raising four kids from nine to eighteen, plus a stretch of years welcoming foster children into our home. We've now run a chore chart at every age you can imagine. Before you start typing dollar figures into the boxes, let me walk you through how we think about money at twelve, because this is the age where getting the money piece right (or wrong) really starts to shape the kind of worker and the kind of person your kid becomes.

sections.heading: How to Set Fair Dollar Amounts (Without Billing Each Chore)
sections.body:
When most of us first picture a chart with money on it, we imagine a tidy price list: dishes earns this, trash earns that, mow the lawn earns the big one. It feels fair and businesslike. The trouble is that a strict price list quietly teaches a twelve-year-old that helping out is a paid gig they can clock in and out of, and at this age they are sharp enough to do the math and decide which chores aren't worth their time.

So here's the approach we'd steer you toward instead. Let the money on the chart reflect how the whole week went, not what each individual job is worth. In our home the amount a kid takes home depends on whether they kept up day after day, did the work to a real standard, and didn't make us chase them for it. The printable gives you a column to write amounts in and a total at the bottom, and we'd encourage you to treat that total as a picture of a solid week rather than an invoice you owe line by line.

A few specifics that have served us well:

- Keep the numbers grounded. A twelve-year-old's chart total should feel like meaningful pocket money, not a salary that lets them buy their way out of pitching in. We started a small weekly allowance back around five or six years old and let it grow with maturity, not just with birthdays.
- Let the total flex. If the week was full of reminders and half-done jobs, the number at the bottom can say so. We tell our kids that's how it works long before it ever happens, so an adjusted total never lands as a nasty surprise.
- Match it to what's actually in reach now. A twelve-year-old can genuinely run the kitchen for an evening, supervise a younger sibling for a bit, or handle a full bathroom clean. The amounts can climb a little as the responsibilities get real.

Think of the dollar figures as a way to make a dependable week visible and worth something, not as a menu your kid orders from one task at a time.

sections.heading: Paid Extra Jobs vs. the Stuff You Do Because You're Family
sections.body:
The single decision that keeps a money chart from turning your house into a marketplace is deciding which chores carry a dollar amount and which simply don't.

In our house, the ordinary running of daily life isn't for sale. Keeping your own room from becoming a disaster, clearing your dishes, wiping down a counter you splattered, tidying the rooms everyone shares: none of that earns a cent. We're pretty plain about why. You're a member of this family, and members of a family take care of the place and each other. When a twelve-year-old has fully absorbed that the basics are just part of belonging here, those jobs stop being something to bargain over, and honestly that lesson is worth more than any allowance.

The money, when it appears, fits better on the bigger optional jobs and on overall reliability. Washing the car, helping clear out the garage, a real yard project, or watching a younger sibling for an afternoon are the kinds of tasks where a dollar value belongs. Our printable lets you mark which rows are paid and which aren't, so that line stays visible right on the chart and your twelve-year-old can see it too.

Twelve is also the launch pad for what comes next. With our teenagers, the chart eventually became impossible to police, so we shifted to something closer to a monthly arrangement: they get a set amount, and in return we can ask for agreed-upon jobs ahead of time, with the month-end figure shrinking if the follow-through fades. That money funds their wants, not their needs, which is the whole reason losing it stings enough to keep them honest. A twelve-year-old isn't quite there, but a money chart that rewards a reliable week is the perfect on-ramp to that more grown-up deal, and your kid will be readier for it because they practiced here first.

sections.heading: Using the Chart to Teach Money Habits (and What to Keep Off It)
sections.body:
A money chart can teach a twelve-year-old genuinely useful things about earning and managing money, but only if you guard it from becoming a machine that dispenses cash and privileges for every behavior.

The best decision we ever made was drawing a hard line between money and two things that have no business near it: screen time and behavior. We don't ask our kids to work in exchange for screens or fun, and we don't shave money off the chart because someone slammed a door or talked back. When there's a real behavior problem, losing screen time is the tool we reach for, and it lives in a completely different lane from the chart and its dollar amounts. The moment those wires cross, a clever twelve-year-old starts negotiating everything in the house, and you've accidentally taught them that money, chores, attitude, and privileges are all one big tradeable currency.

A few habits that have worked for us:

- Make the weekly total a conversation, not just a payout. When the number is lower than usual, talk about what got in the way. The teaching happens there, not in the handing over of cash.
- Keep treats in their own bucket. With our younger kids we've kept a cheap prize box they can pick from now and then for work done well and with a good attitude, deliberately walled off from the chart's money so it never reads as a bribe.
- Let them own what the money is for. At twelve, the things they're saving toward (a game, an outing with friends, that one thing they keep mentioning) are what make the habit stick. We cover the needs; the chart funds the wants they actually care about.

One thing our years as foster parents drove home: for kids who'd arrived from homes without much steady structure, the chart's real gift was never the money on it. It was the predictability. Knowing what was expected and trusting that the rules wouldn't shift on them helped those kids steady themselves and feel like part of the household far faster than we expected. You don't have to be fostering for that to matter. Even with a confident twelve-year-old, the dependable structure of a chart you actually keep up with is doing the heavy lifting, and the money is just a small, useful layer riding on top of it.

faq.q: How much should I pay a 12-year-old for chores?
faq.a: We'd keep it modest and tie it to the whole week rather than to each task. In our house allowance started small around five or six years old and grows with maturity, so by twelve it's meaningful pocket money but not a paycheck. We don't run a per-chore price list; the amount reflects whether the week's work was done well, kept up day to day, and done without being chased. The printable here lets you set your own figures in the money column and watch them add up to a weekly total.

faq.q: Should a 12-year-old be paid for every chore?
faq.a: In our home, no. The everyday running of the house, like a kid's own room, their dishes, and the shared spaces they use, stays unpaid because pitching in is part of being family, not a transaction. We attach money mainly to bigger optional jobs and to overall reliability. The chart lets you mark which rows are paid and which aren't, so your twelve-year-old can see exactly where the line sits between extra work and the basics everyone is expected to handle.

faq.q: Is a chore chart with money still a good idea at this age, or should I switch to allowance?
faq.a: At twelve, a money chart is a great bridge between the two. It still gives you a visible record of how the week went, which is the chart's real value to you as a parent, while introducing the idea that money follows dependable follow-through. With our teenagers we eventually dropped the chart for a monthly job-style arrangement, but a twelve-year-old usually isn't ready for that yet. A chart whose money column rewards a steady week is the perfect practice run for the more independent setup that comes later.
